Items.Authors: Lorenzo Pettazzi, Martin Dimmler, Mauro Tuti, Omar Sqalli, Andreas Foerster, Marc Cayrel
Items.Title: Serial production in the context of ground-based astronomy projects: the ELT M1 case
Items.Abstract: The M1 is, without a doubt, one of the most impressive subsystems within the ELT telescope. The endeavor of building such a masterpiece of technology is tightly linked to the challenges of designing, developing and producing in series the hundreds or thousands of components that constitute the gigantic active mirror. This manuscript focuses on the description of the multiple challenges that ESO and its industrial partners have faced to ensure that the design of the M1 components was properly engineered for serial production, to set up the production facilities and to maintain the specified production quality and yield over the years. Finally the paper will describe the multiple solutions adopted in the different projects to overcome the challenges and reflects on the lessons learned during the process.

Items.Authors: Schuyler G. Wolff, Vanessa Bailey, Justin Hom, Maxwell A. Millar-Blanchaer, Susan F. Redmond, Julien H. Girard, Oscar Carrión-González, Dmitry Savransky, Johan Mazoyer, Macarena Vega-Pallauta, Gael Chauvin, Matthieu Ravet, Alexandra Greenbaum, Eric Cady, Ramya M. Anche, James G. Ingalls
Items.Title: The Roman Coronagraph Community Participation Program: trials and triumphs of designing an observing program for a technology demonstration instrument
Items.Abstract: The Coronagraph Instrument onboard the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope serves as a crucial technology pathfinder for the Habitable Worlds Observatory, with on-sky verification of high-contrast imaging techniques and the potential to image a Jupiter analog for the first time. Together with the Roman Project Team, the Community Participation Program (CPP) is responsible for target selection, preparatory observations, developing an exposure time calculator, target database, data reduction pipeline, simulation tools, and engagement with the broader community. Here we present an overview of the CPP activities over the past two years with an emphasis on observation planning activities for the initial in-orbit checkout and the first six months of the observation phase. Finally, we present future opportunities for the astronomical community to interact with the data as it becomes public early in the mission.

Items.Authors: Felicia Carla Tiziana Barbato
Items.Title: Crystal eye: real time localization of gamma ray transients
Items.Abstract: Crystal Eye is a new space-based all-sky monitor designed to detect 10 keV–30 MeV photons using advanced scintillator crystals and high-efficiency silicon photomultipliers. It offers improved localization and sensitivity for short astrophysical transients, enabling real-time alerts that support multi-messenger observations. The full-scale detector design has been optimized, and an engineering qualification model is in development. A smaller prototype consisting of three full-size pixels will fly on ESA’s Space Rider in 2027 to characterize the orbital background and validate the technology. We present the instrument concept and expected performance based on full-detector Monte Carlo simulations and prototype tests.

Items.Authors: Sven C. Herrmann, Peter Orel, Tanmoy Chattopadhyay, R. Glenn Morris, Haley R. Stueber, Abigail Y. Pan, Declan O'Neill, Sebastian Albrecht, Steven W. Allen, Marshall W. Bautz, Michael J. Cooper, Ajay K. Dakshinamurthy, Kevan A. Donlon, Catherine E. Grant, Matthew Heine, Jill Juneau, Beverly J. LaMarr, Christopher W. Leitz, Eric D. Miller, Artem Poliszczuk, Gregory Y. Prigozhin, Anna Schweingruber, Keith Warner, Daniel R. Wilkins
Items.Title: Fast, low noise, megapixel detector and readout systems for future X-ray astronomy missions
Items.Abstract: State-of-the-art X-ray CCDs are close to delivering the key performance metrics for the next generation of X-ray telescope except the required frame rates. Our group at Stanford is addressing these technology gaps, in collaboration with colleagues at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) and MIT Lincoln Laboratory (MIT-LL). To meet this need, we are developing advanced multichannel readout electronics that utilize microelectronics, waveform sampling, and digital signal processing in an FPGA. First operation with a large 2 Mpixel MIT-LL CCD was achieved and demonstrates the performance of this architecture. We also report progress on our continued development of the novel SiSeRO (Single electron Sensitive Read Out) technology, which can deliver substantially sub-electron noise at competitive readout speeds. Finally, we discuss the development of AI methods to enhance our detector performance, including enhanced particle background screening and improved event characterization.

Items.Authors: John Romein, Ewan Barr, Ilse van Bemmel, Wiebe van Breukelen, Théo Chicard, Willem-Jan Dirks, Hugh Garsden, André Gunst, Valentin Hazard, Aard Keimpema, Mark Kettenis, Corné Lukken, Jan David Mol, Leon Oostrum, Vishambhar Nath Pandey, Matīss Purviņš, Benjamin Quertier, Ronald Rook, Theotime Sergeant, Jānis Šteinbergs, Gie Han Tan, Bram Veenboer, Marjolein Verkouter, Eric Villard, Steven van der Vlugt
Items.Title: RADIOBLOCKS: High-performance building blocks for GPU correlators
Items.Abstract: In this session, we present RADIOBLOCKS: a collection of highly optimized GPU signal-processing libraries, that form the building blocks for a new generation of radio-astronomical correlator and beam-former applications. We also describe new methods to efficiently transfer data from FPGA digitizers near the antennas into GPU correlator systems, at high data rates. Finally, we show how these "radio blocks" and I/O methods are deployed in (upgrades of) correlator/beam-former applications for a variety of radio telescopes.

Items.Authors: Arjo Bos, Pim van Wershoven, Bart Speet, Fred Kamphues, Wouter Jonker
Items.Title: Sensitivity analysis and design of a segmented active M1 for the next-generation telescopes
Items.Abstract: In the current generation of Extremely Large Telescopes (ELTs), relatively thick segmented M1 mirror segments are applied. These mirror segments of significant mass have complex mechanical support structures that warp and co-phase each element such that a single mirror surface is achieved. TNO believes that with recent developments, the next-generation telescopes can be made possible by decreasing mass, making the M1 segments active (or even adaptive), and significantly decreasing the cost of the glass mirror segments.   In this publication we present a sensitivity analysis and concept design of a segmented active thin-shell M1 segment for the next-generation telescopes. Multiple applications are foreseen, from retrofitting existing telescopes such as a 15m Keck 2.0, application in the Wide-Field Spectroscopic Telescope (WST), or even a 60+ meter ELT.

Items.Authors: Marianne Cox, Jose M. Filgueira, Chien Peng, Jordi Molgó, Hector Swett, Jorge Barrios, Gibreel El-Halabi, Paulo H. Silva
Items.Title: Observatory software management in the era of AI-assisted software engineering
Items.Abstract: Thanks to advancements in generative AI and Large Language Models (LLMs), the last 5 years has seen exponential growth in the adoption of AI-Assisted Software Engineering (AISE) across many industries. Simple developer tools used for code completion, static analysis and syntax linting, have been replaced by agent-assisted development and autonomous coding. The way we develop, analyze and test software is rapidly changing.   At GMTO, we believe that we stand to benefit from staying up to date with these technologies and adopting AISE best practices. However, it needs to be done in a way that carefully considers our unique concerns and risks. In this paper we describe how we are starting to utilize AISE at GMTO, why common industry concerns matter for Observatory software teams, and potential mitigations and lessons learned thus far.

Items.Authors: Justin Hom, Schuyler G. Wolff, Jessica Gersh-Range, Ramya M. Anche, Vanessa P. Bailey, Jean-Philippe Berger, Beth A. Biller, Wolfgang Brandner, Marah Brinjikji, Gaël Chauvin, Catherine A. Clark, Robert J. De Rosa, Julien H. Girard, Alexandra Z. Greenbaum, Masayuki Kuzuhara, Manon Lallement, Jean-Baptiste Le Bouquin, Eric Mamajek, Bruce Macintosh, Maxwell A. Millar-Blanchaer, Toshiyuki Mizuki, Nicholas T. Schragal, Macarena C. Vega-Pallauta, Jason J. Wang, Jingwen Zhang
Items.Title: The Roman Coronagraph Community Participation Program: pre-launch reference star list and impact of reference star properties on post-processing performance
Items.Abstract: The upcoming Roman Coronagraph aims to directly image and characterize exoplanetary systems at contrasts higher than 10^-7, a key technological milestone for Habitable Worlds Observatory coronagraph development. Doing so requires alternating observations of science targets and bright reference stars. These reference stars must satisfy strict criteria, including being single star systems. Other reference star attributes may have other impacts on post-processing performance on a case-by-case basis. Only a small number of the brightest stars in the sky are potentially suitable, necessitating precursor observations and simulations to validate their use. We will present the pre-launch list of Roman Coronagraph reference stars informed from an extensive observing campaign. We will also present the results of simulations investigating the impact of reference star properties on post-processing performance. We discuss the importance of reference star selection for scheduling and performance.

Items.Authors: Heidi Schweiker, William McBride
Items.Title: Using field mills to monitor atmospheric electric fields for lightning safety at observatories
Items.Abstract: For remote mountain-top observatories, lightning is a considerable risk to personnel and hardware. Conventional lightning warnings are often inaccurate or too late for a timely response. In order to get a more precise indication of the potential for a lightning strike, we have installed field mills to monitor the electric fields in the atmosphere above Kitt Peak National Observatory. Regularly in use for rocket launches and (previously) the Space Shuttle, field mills can indicate a buildup of electrical charge, which is a known precursor to a lightning strike. We will discuss the deployment and integration of our field mills with our mountain operations, the development of thresholds for automatic broadcast alerts and safety precautions we have incorporated in response to these alerts. Based on our experience we will present how other observatories can benefit from incorporating similar electric field monitoring systems into their operations and safety programs.

Items.Authors: Bernadett Stadler, Guido Agapito, Ollie Farley, Noelia Martinez Rey, Alfio Puglisi, Fabio Rossi, Roberto Biasi, Domenico Bonaccini Calia, David Jenkins, Daniel Jodlbauer, Ramon Mata Calvo, James Osborn, Felipe Pedreros Bustos
Items.Title: End-to-end adaptive optics simulations for predicting the performance of bidirectional optical feeder links
Items.Abstract: Space optical laser communication represents a technological challenge. Atmospheric turbulence disturbs the uplink and downlink laser beams, thus, strongly limiting the achievable data throughput. In this talk we focus on the prediction of the performance improvement when employing Adaptive Optics (AO) systems for the optical communication with GEO and LEO satellites using numerical end-to-end simulations. In particular, we show results for the ALASCA project, which develops an optical communication channel from the ESA optical ground station in Tenerife to communication satellites using the Laser Guide Star AO (LGS-AO) concept. The simulations are carried out using SPECULA, which is a Python-based end-to-end AO software tool developed at INAF Arcetri for astronomical applications that has been adapted for the use in optical communication. The reliability of the simulations is guaranteed through cross-validation with other numerical and analytical simulators as well as on-sky results.

Items.Authors: Patrick Côté, Tyrone E. Woods, Matthew A. Taylor, John S. Pazder
Items.Title: Progress report on the CASTOR mission
Items.Abstract: We present a progress report on the CASTOR mission. CASTOR is a proposed 1m-diameter, wide-field space telescope that is under development by the National Research Council of Canada and the Canadian Space Agency. The mission utilizes a three-mirror anastigmat design to deliver high-resolution imaging (FWHM ~0.15”) over a ~0.25 square degree field simultaneously in three channels: UV (150-300nm), u (300-400nm) and g (400-550nm). The telescope will be mounted on the Magellan MAC-200 small-SAT bus, and placed into a sun-synchronous dawn-dusk orbit at an altitude of roughly 800 km. According to the current development schedule, launch would occur in the early 2030s.    The mission design is optimized for panoramic imaging in three simultaneous channels covering the UV/blue-optical wavelength range. Additional observing modes include: (1) wide-field, slit-less (grism) spectroscopy between 150 and 400 nm; (2) precision photometry for exoplanet transit measurements; and (3) DMD-based UV multi-

Items.Authors: Sebastian Schäfer, Michael Debus, Tobias Schmidt, Vitalii Kostogryz, Ansgar Reiners
Items.Title: Toward a community framework for illumination stability in EPRV spectrographs
Items.Abstract: As extreme-precision RV spectrographs push toward the 10 cm/s regime, illumination stability has become a dominant but poorly quantified limitation. At present, every major EPRV instrument team develops its own set of scrambling metrics, fiber tests, and modal-noise mitigation strategies. These efforts have led to impressive individual results, but they are not directly comparable, and they do not yet form a transferable framework that new instruments can adopt without repeating large parts of the experimental work.  We introduce an effort to establish reproducible illumination metrics. Rather than instrument-specific tests, we will map illumination behaviour across a broad range of wavelengths, source types, fibers, and launch conditions to capture the diversity of real systems. Our goal is to provide illumination metrics and guidelines that can be shared, compared, and reused, reducing duplicated effort and supporting the design of future high-precision radial-velocity instruments.

Items.Authors: Michael Pleasance
Items.Title: Correlator/beamformer for the Square Kilometre Array Mid Frequency Telescope: design and status update
Items.Abstract: The National Research Council of Canada (NRC) is leading the development and delivery of the Square Kilometer Array (SKA) Mid Frequency Correlator/Beamformer (Mid.CBF) signal processing system. This talk provides an overview of the system design for both the early prototype systems (TALON Demonstration Correlator) and production systems for the larger array assemblies. The talk also provides a status update, highlighting completed and upcoming milestones.

Items.Authors: Rodolphe Conan, Konstantinos Vogiatzsis, Henry Fitzpatrick, Christoph Dribusch, Rodrigo Romano
Items.Title: Dome seeing and wind jitter estimation for the GMT Final Design
Items.Abstract: The Giant Magellan Telescope (GMT) has reached its final design phase with many subsystems either working towards or having already completed their final design. Dome seeing and telescope wind jitter are critical consideration for the design of many subsystems. The GMT has performed an extensive Computational Fluids Dynamic (CFD) simulation campaign to verify the compliance of the Observatory final design with respect to the GMT Key Performance Parameters (KPP).     The paper gives an overview of the CFD observatory model and describes the derivation processes for both the dome seeing and the wind jitter from the CFD data. The dome seeing results are presented in the context of the Natural Seeing observing mode of the GMT. The wind jitter analysis is performed considering the compensation of the image jitter with the GMT Adaptive Optics systems .Finally, the compliance of the telescope final design with respect to the dome seeing and wind jitter KPPs is summarized.

Items.Authors: Julian Cuevas-Zepeda, Joseph Noonan, Juan Estrada, Miguel Sofo-Haro, Claudio Chavez, Nathan Saffold
Items.Title: Fully depleted, low-noise 725-micron thick p-channel SiSeRO for 5-20 keV X-ray detection
Items.Abstract: The p-channel Single-electron Sensitive Readout (SiSeRO) CCD is a fully-depleted, 725-µm-thick sensor fabricated at MIT Lincoln Laboratory, capable of achieving sub-electron noise with repetitive non-destructive readout (NDR) faster than a Skipper CCD. The device employs a double-gate n-MOSFET amplifier, which has previously proven to achieve high-fidelity pixel readout speeds—-in both single-sample and non-destructive readout modes—that are at least 6x faster than floating-gate amplifier CCDs. In this work we present the X-ray energy response of the n-SiSeRO. Using Fe-55, we measure the energy resolution of the Mn Kα peak at 15.8 e- in single-sample mode and 14.6 e- with 100-sample NDR. We further demonstrate sensitivity up to 60 keV with Am-241, resolving fluorescence features between 9–26 keV.

Items.Authors: Sorabh Chhabra, Stefan Kraus, Daniel Lancaster, Jyotirmay Paul, Michele Frangiamore, Andrea Bianco, Michael Ireland, Owain Snaith
Items.Title: Integration and commissioning of the ASGARD/BIFROST low-resolution (R ≈ 50–5000) spectrograph at the VLTI
Items.Abstract: The BIFROST, part of the Asgard instrument suite for the VLTI, offers spectro-interferometric capabilities across the Y, J, and H bands. We here report on the commissioning of the low-resolution spectrograph arm of BIFROST. We describe the integration of the spectrograph on site, the alignment procedure, and the first on-sky tests performed with the VLTI auxiliary/ unit telescopes. Using standard calibration sources and stellar targets, we characterize the achieved spectral throughput, background levels, calibration stability, and spectral resolution in the low-resolution modes (R ≈ 50, R950 and R5000). We also compare results with pre-commissioning laboratory expectations.

Items.Authors: Renaud Mercier-Ythier, Gilles Chaussat, Frédéric Boillet, Christophe Couteret, Aurélie Delfosse, Dimitri Estevez, Marc Gouedard, Cyril Mugnier
Items.Title: Manufacturing the ELT M1 segments: achieving optimized production in a smart factory
Items.Abstract: In 2017, the European Southern Observatory (ESO) awarded Safran Reosc the contract for polishing, integration, and final figuring of the Segment Assemblies for the ELT's primary mirror (M1). Production began in 2022 and has now reached full pace, with over 600 segments expected to be produced by the end of 2025, out of the total 931 required. With a rate of one segment per day, seven days a week, completion is scheduled for early 2027. This article presents the advancements in manufacturing processes and the smart factory organization implemented to optimize production and achieve high throughput, while maintaining the high performance requested by ESO.

Items.Authors: Thierry Fusco, Nicolas Vedrenne, Benoît Neichel, Jean-François Sauvage, Pierre-Louis Mayeur, Cyril Petit
Items.Title: Adaptive optics for astronomy, defense, and free-space optics: complementarities, synergies, and specificities
Items.Abstract: Adaptive optics (AO), conceived by Babcock in 1953, became practical in the 1970–80s through major U.S. defense advances in deformable mirrors, wavefront sensing, and real-time control. Transposed into astronomy, AO achieved its first on-sky demonstration in 1989 at the Haute-Provence Observatory and is now essential for large telescopes, especially future 30–40 m ELTs. Key breakthroughs—laser guide stars, fast low-noise detectors, and high-actuator-density deformable mirrors—enable near full-sky coverage and diffraction-limited performance. Beyond astronomy, AO is central to defense and free-space optical communications, stabilizing ground-to-satellite laser links via advanced sensing and turbulence prediction. In this presentation, I will outline the intertwined evolution of these fields, highlighting strong technological synergies that establish AO as a strategic and multidisciplinary technology, and illustrate this with emblematic examples.

Items.Authors: Alejandro F. Saez, Tzu-Chiang Shen, Theodoros Nakos, Juan Cortes, Matias Radiszcz
Items.Title: Assembly, integration, and verification (AIV) planning for implementing the ALMA wideband sensitivity upgrade (WSU) project.
Items.Abstract: The ALMA telescope has been operating for more than a decade and is now undergoing an upgrade to enhance its capabilities in line with advances in electronics. The primary goal is to at least double the instantaneous bandwidth, with a stretch goal of achieving a fourfold increase.    A major challenge is ensuring uninterrupted operations while the required retrofitting is performed. This effort involves upgrading the instrumentation in the array elements, deploying new data-transmission infrastructure, and installing the new correlator.    This work summarizes the key constraints of the upgrade, outlines the strategies, technical considerations, and tactical decisions adopted, and presents a framework for estimating the required effort and timeline for completing the defined stages.

Items.Authors: Reinder Kraaij, Jun Wang, Henk Mulder
Items.Title: Being a developer between science and operations
Items.Abstract: A journey into being a developer in the middle of the science world, assisting all sides to create a operable radio telescope, by the hand of a real world story about the creation of the LOFAR 2.0 real-time analysing of the station signals, resulting in aggregated system-health metrics, giving you tips to tackle this dynamic world between science, development and operations.

Items.Authors: Yong Chen, Dawei Han, Juan Wang, Weiwei Cui, Xiaofan Zhao, Juan Zhang, Yanji Yang, Shumei Jia, Chengkui Li, Jingjing Xu, Guangxueying Wan, Jiaxiong Sun, Siyuan Sun
Items.Title: Observational capabilities and highlights of the FengXingTian space X-ray telescope for diffuse sources
Items.Abstract: As the follow-up X-ray telescope onboard the Tianguan（EP）satellite, the FengXingTian (FXT) has been operational in orbit for two years, demonstrating excellent performance. FXT features a wide field of view measuring 1°x1°, an effective area of 600 square centimeters, and an energy resolution of approximately 100 eV at 1.5 keV. Operating in low Earth orbit, the FXT's Wolter-I type focusing mirror has a very short focal length of only 1.6 meters. This design allows FXT to use a smaller detector area compared to long-focal-length telescopes when observing diffuse objects of the same scale. Additionally, FXT is equipped with sets of permanent magnet-based electron deflectors at both the exit of the focusing mirror and the entrance of the detector, effectively reducing the background noise caused by high-energy electrons in orbit. These features endow FXT with strong capabilities for observing diffuse sources. In orbit, FXT has successfully observed numerous celestial bodies, including gal

Items.Authors: Julien H. Girard, Eric Cady, Neil T. Zimmerman, Gael Chauvin, Vanessa Bailey, Ruslan Belikov, Beth Biller, Sarah Blunt, Jessica Gersh-Range, Justin Hom, Masayuki Kuzuhara, Maxwell A. Millar-Blanchaer, Matthias Samland, Dan Sirbu, Macarena Vega-Pallauta, Schuyler G. Wolff, Jason Wang, Jingwen Zhang
Items.Title: The Roman Coronagraph Community Participation Program: end to end preparation of a pilot observation of a moderate contrast companion
Items.Abstract: The Coronagraph Instrument, technology pathfinder, is ready to fly onboard the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, a NASA flagship mission scheduled to launch before the Spring 2027. The Community Participation Program (CPP) is building a comprehensive observing program for the “Coronagraph” with preparation, calibration and data processing software. Here we describe a sub-program that could be carried out as soon as the instrument is operational and high-order wavefront sensing and control has been exercised successfully. This program would generate the first canonical on-sky dataset of a bright star with an easily recoverable self luminous companion. We show all preparation steps using the whole suite of tools developed by the CPP. This “training” dataset will be precious for the readiness of the technology demonstration at higher contrasts and for our community to subsequently tackle more difficult targets, including giant exoplanets in reflected light.

Items.Authors: Mirka Lewińska-Maresca, Dennis Dolkens, Niels Tromp, Joost van den Born, Jeff Lynn, Rik ter Horst, Menno de Haan, Juan-Pablo Garcia, Ties van Loon, Sander Paalvast, Martijn Denissen, Maurice Teuwen, Remco de Bruijn, Niels Bouman, Shiang-Yu Wang, Elfi Dijkstra, Menno Schuil, Gerard van Egmond, Peter Kunst, Jan Rinze Peterzon, Eddy Elswijk
Items.Title: High-speed and high-stability cryogenic beam chopping with the METIS cold chopper
Items.Abstract: The METIS Cold Chopper (MCC) is a key component of the Mid-infrared ELT Imager and Spectrograph (METIS). At infrared wavelengths, rapid subtraction of the bright, variable background is essential. The MCC provides this via a cryogenic tip/tilt mirror with a cold-stop mask. By tilting around two axes, it redirects the beam between the science target and reference sky positions within the chop throw, enabling efficient background suppression without moving the telescope. In post-processing, each target frame is paired with a sky exposure, and thousands of sky-subtracted images are co-added.    Demanding requirements shape the MCC hardware and control design: fast beam switching with short settling times, high positional repeatability for long integrations, and strong thermal and vibrational stability for robust control. These needs require tightly coordinated development of mechanics, electronics, software, and control. This paper outlines the MCC design and key verification results

Items.Authors: Ewelina Obrzud, Tobias Schmidt, François Bouchy, Gaspare Lo Curto, Victor Brasch, Tobias Herr, Furkan Ayhan, Séverine Denis, Davide Grassani, Jean Berney, Bruno Chazelas, Weichen Fan, Jannis Holzer, Ian Hughes, Markus Ludwig, Antonio Manescau, Luca Pasquini, Francesco Pepe, Guillermo Villanueva, Thibaut Wildi
Items.Title: Test of an electro-optic 34 GHz astrocomb at ESPRESSO
Items.Abstract: Laser frequency combs, producing a dense grid of equidistant optical emission lines, are considered the best calibration sources for precision astronomical spectrographs. Here we present results of a testing campaign of an electro-optic astrocomb at the ESPRESSO spectrograph and highlight the development of thin-film lithium niobate integrated waveguides for generation of spectra spanning from the near-UV, through the visible and into the near-infrared.

Items.Authors: Dean Howarth, Vikram Ravi
Items.Title: Accelerating dedispersion for fast transient detection in radio astronomy using tensor core GPU architecture
Items.Abstract: The Deep Synoptic Array (DSA), completing in 2028 with 1650 dishes, will survey the 0.7-2GHz band to discover 10^5 Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs) and 22,000 pulsars. We present the DSA Chronoscope, an instrument designed to search six million beams for FRBs and 2×10^5 for pulsars using rack-scale NVIDIA Vera Rubin GPUs. Addressing data streams that exceed conventional capabilities, we detail visibility-based beamforming and dedispersion implementations utilizing FFTs and batched GEMMs to leverage NVIDIA Tensor Cores. Using cuFFT and CUTLASS/cuBLASLt with precision down-casting, our novel restructuring of Frequency Domain Dedispersion (FDD) and Fast Dispersion Measure Transform (FDMT) algorithms achieves a 1000-fold increase in arithmetic intensity. This optimization increases throughput to tens of thousands of beams per GPU.

Items.Authors: Mahy Soler, Javier Rodríguez, Luis Lacoma, Antonio Zamora, Juan Cózar-Castellano
Items.Title: Characterization of internal local seeing in the European Solar Telescope: from transfer optics to Coudé rooms
Items.Abstract: The European Solar Telescope (EST) targets diffraction-limited performance, establishing "local seeing" minimization as a primary engineering objective. Complementing previous external studies, this work characterizes the critical internal optical path: the Transfer Optics and Calibration Assembly (TOCA) and Coudé Light Distribution (CLD).   An integrated CFD and optical simulation framework is applied to evaluate the TOCA interface trade-off between an air-knife system and a solid window. Furthermore, the analysis extends to the Coudé Rooms, assessing thermal gradients generated by electronics and HVAC systems along the distinct Visible and Infrared paths. Key metrics, including Optical Path Difference (OPD) and Fried parameter, are derived. These results verify the internal thermal control strategies, ensuring the EST design meets the image quality requirements.

Items.Authors: Nicolas De Angelis, Sergio Fabiani, Ettore Del Monte, Giovanni Lombardi, Abhay Kumar
Items.Title: Compton Polarimeter Prototype for the CUbesat Solar Polarimeter (CUSP) mission
Items.Abstract: The space-based CUbesat Solar Polarimeter (CUSP) mission aims to measure the linear polarization of solar flares in the hard X-ray band (25-100~keV) by means of a dual-phase Compton polarimeter. CUSP will allow to study the magnetic reconnection and particle acceleration in the flaring magnetic structures of our star with its unprecedented sensitivity to solar flare polarization. CUSP is a project under development as part of the Alcor Program of the Italian Space Agency aimed at developing new CubeSat missions.    In the frame of CUSP's Phase B, a representative prototype of the Compton polarimeter has been developed and characterized with hard X-ray sources in the laboratory. This prototype consists of a 4x4 central matrix of plastic scintillator bars surrounded by 4 strips of 8 elongated GAGG scintillators, respectively coupled to a multi-anode photomultiplier tube and arrays of avalanche photodiodes. We report here the measured performances of the polarimeter prototype.

Items.Authors: Jacob Isbell, Steve Ertel, Fernando Pedichini
Items.Title: LBT Interferometer Visible Extension (LIVE): pioneering thirty-meter-class telescope imaging in the visible
Items.Abstract: Combining the light from two 8.4 m mirrors, the Large Binocular Telescope (LBT) Interferometer achieves imaging resolution equivalent to that of a 28.8 m telescope via Fizeau interferometry. A newly NSF/ATI-funded instrument, the LBT Interferometer Visible Extension (LIVE), will bring these capabilities to visible wavelengths for the first time.     LIVE will be optimized for Hɑ (656 nm) – achieving 5 milliarcsecond imaging resolution – but will also operate from 600-1000 nm. LIVE makes use of existing LBTI infrastructure, serving as a pathfinder for a future standalone visible-light Fizeau instrument at the LBT. Because the LBT is in many ways the first thirty-meter-class telescope in operation, LIVE can both pioneer and complement future science with the ELT and GMT. The combination of high sensitivity and high resolution that the LBT Interferometer can provide – from visible to infrared – will open new parameter spaces to explore.

Items.Authors: Ralph P. Kraft, Caroline A. Kilbourne, Simon R. Bandler, Akos Bogdan, Renata S. Cumbee, Megan E. Eckart, Edmund Hodges-Kluck, Richard L. Kelley, Maurice Andrew Leutenegger, Daniel McCammon, Daisuke Nagai, Anna Ogorzalek, Takashi Okajima, Naomi Ota, Daniel J. Patnaude, Frederick Scott Porter, Paul Plucinsky, Kosuke Sato, Gerrit Schellenberger, Malgorzata Sobolewska, Hiroyuki Uchida, Hiroya Yamaguchi, Noriko Y. Yamasaki, Irina Zhuravleva, John A. Zuhone
Items.Title: The Explorer for Cosmic Ecosystems and Energetic Dynamics (ExCEED) mission concept
Items.Abstract: We present the Explorer for Cosmic Ecosystems and Energetic Dynamics – a mission concept under development for the next MIDEX AO. The ExCEED mission consists of one science instrument combining a wide-field soft X-ray optic and a high-spectral resolution imaging microcalorimeter array. ExCEED will operate in a low-inclination, Low-Earth Orbit (LEO) to maximize rapid ToO capability, minimize particle background, and allow for a simple and inexpensive spacecraft. The microcalorimeter will be based on the same pixel design as the NewAthena XIFU instrument but optimized for lower energies. We are pursuing an X-ray optic from COSINE based on the silicon pore optic technology, drawing heritage from the large ESA investment in NewAthena. The ExCEED team is an international collaboration including major partners from SAO, GSFC, and ISAS. The Directed and General Observer science of ExCEED will span priority science themes and discovery areas outlined in the Astro2020 Decadal.

Items.Authors: Jan Kinast, Melanie Ulitschka, Markus Unger, Ralf Steinkopf, Tatjana Porwol, Luxuan Cai, Robert Jende, Sandra Müller, Mathias Rohde, Nancy Ageorges, Florian Lang, Lenard Spallek, Yixian Cao, Kateryna Kravchenko, Federico Biondi, Michael Hartl, Sebastian Rabien, Andreas Kamm, Thomas Peschel, Stefan Risse
Items.Title: Dimensional stability of a direct polished aluminum mirror substrate at 82 K
Items.Abstract: MICADO (Multi-AO Imaging Camera for Deep Observations) is a first light instrument for the Extremely Large Telescope (ELT). Fraunhofer IOF is responsible for four optical-mechanical systems for MICADO: COL, HRI, LRI, and CAM. The opto-mechanical systems operate at 82 K to avoid thermal radiation. To validate the suitability of the metal optics used, a representative mirror is tested for dimensional stability. This mirror, made from RSA6061, is manufactured using CNC milling, diamond turning, ion beam figuring (IBF), and chemical-mechanical polishing (CMP). After thermal treatments, the dimensional stability is analyzed by interferometric measurements. Fraunhofer IOF investigates plastic dimensional stability at ambient conditions after thermal cycles, while the Max Planck Institute investigates thermally induced deformations in a vacuum chamber at operational temperature. The paper discusses the ultra-precise machining and dimensional stability of RSA6061 under cryogenic conditions.

Items.Authors: James D. Neill
Items.Title: Growing a software group at the Caltech Optical Observatories
Items.Abstract: The Caltech Optical Observatories has recently expanded their software team from two to seven software engineers by hiring junior and senior engineers from industry. Our aim is to improve our development process with knowledge of practices from the wider software engineering industry in combination with the instrument software experience from our existing engineers. We have a set of goals to achieve an improved process and contribute to the community by presenting software tools that are of general use. We also hope to host workshops focused on instrument control software and standards that will enhance collaboration and code reuse. I will discuss the process of integrating industry practices into our group and will enumerate the software tools that are presented elsewhere at this meeting.

Items.Authors: Hyeonho Choi, Myungshin Im, Ji Hoon Kim, Donggeun Tak, Seo-Won Chang, Seong-Kook Joshua Lee
Items.Title: RTCSpy: A Robotic Telescope Control System for Multi-Telescope Array with Sub-Minute ToO Response
Items.Abstract: We present RTCSpy, a network-based robotic telescope control system for fully autonomous operation of multi-telescope arrays. RTCSpy provides end-to-end automation—including startup, calibration, observation and shutdown—while coordinating all telescope units through real-time, network-based communication. Its operational framework integrates both synchronized control and automated decision-making by evaluating target priorities, available resources, and weather conditions within a unified queue-based framework, while a dedicated Target of Opportunity(ToO) manager monitors external alerts and enables sub-minute interruption for rapid transient response. Deployed since August 2023 on the 7-Dimensional Telescope(7DT), RTCSpy has demonstrated stable nightly operation and reliable rapid-response performance. Its network-based architecture also supports straightforward expansion to additional units and multi-site arrays, enabling coordinated observations across distributed facilities.

Items.Authors: Jason J. Wang, Maxwell A. Millar-Blanchaer, Marie Ygouf, Sergi Hildebrandt, Julia Milton, Juergen Schreiber, Ell Bogat, Kevin Ludwick, Amanda Chavez, Eric Shen, Ramya Anche, Toshiyuki Mizuki, Taichi Uyama, Ezar Shinbaro, Neil Zimmerman, Alexis Lau, William Balmer, Ben Sutlieff, Matthias Samland, A. J. Eldorado Riggs, Lisa Altinier, Sophie Noiret, Kylee Fluckiger, Clarissa Do Ó, Malachi Noel, Dmitry Savransky, Michele Woodland, John Livingston, Tsutsumi Nagai, Al Niessner, Cynthia Wong, Eric Cady, Guillermo Gonzalez, Alexandra Z. Greenbaum, Jingwen Zhang, Vanessa Bailey
Items.Title: The Roman Coronagraph Community Participation Program: data reduction pipeline design and implementation
Items.Abstract: The Roman Space Telescope Coronagraph Instrument will demonstrate a series of technologies and techniques to enable the direct detection of reflected-light planets with space-based observatories. To characterize and validate the performance of the Coronagraph Instrument, the Community Participation Program is developing corgidrp, an open-source Python-based data reduction pipeline. The pipeline can process data from the required and best-effort observing modes and their associated calibration sequences. We present the software design and implementation of corgidrp. We describe the software architecture, data flow, processing steps, automation tools, testing framework, and development philosophy. We will also outline future development plans in preparation for on-sky data.

Items.Authors: Andrea Pertoldi, Niccolò Barberio, Francesco Canella, Benjamin Rudin, Florian Emaury, Francesco Benatti, Dario Giannotti, Francesco Leone, Paolo Laporta, Gianluca Galzerano
Items.Title: A broadband 10 GHz astrocomb for high-resolution spectrograph calibration
Items.Abstract: We demonstrate a fully stabilized astrocomb based on a compact 10 GHz mode-locked laser designed for calibrating high-resolution astronomical spectrographs. A dual-stage all-fiber amplifier supports stable f–2f self-referencing and broadband coherent supercontinuum generation, while an additional visible arm extends the comb to provide continuous 10 GHz-spaced lines across both the VIS and NIR spectral regions. We report a full characterization of the system’s optical, RF, and environmental performance over multi-day operation, demonstrating excellent robustness, low phase noise, and stable long-term behavior suitable for observatory deployment.

Items.Authors: Nithyanandan Thyagarajan, Jishnu Thekkeppattu, David Humphrey
Items.Title: A fast, wide-field, and real-time imaging prototype for large aperture arrays
Items.Abstract: Real-time, sub-millisecond processing is crucial for detecting extreme astrophysical events such as fast radio bursts, enabling instant localisation and rapid follow-up. Large-N aperture arrays like SKA-low, ASKAP, CHIME, CHORD, MWA, and LOFAR rely on this. But processing using traditional correlators scales as O(N²), creating computational, bandwidth, and power bottlenecks. Direct imaging techniques, which bypass pairwise correlations, offer a scalable alternative. The E-field Parallel Imaging “Correlator” (EPIC) achieves O(N log N) scaling and has been demonstrated on the LWA–Sevilleta using GPUs, though GPU memory bandwidth limits performance. This work explores an FPGA-based EPIC, using fully parallel FFT pipelines to reduce power consumption while maintaining high-speed processing. We evaluate performance, scalability, and energy efficiency, highlighting the potential for next-generation large-N aperture arrays to expand discovery space and enable large-scale, real-time astronomy.

Items.Authors: Alexei Ippa, Christoph Tamm, Stefan Thoms, Eberhard Sust
Items.Title: Dynamic simulations for the CTA large sized telescope - south
Items.Abstract: The Large Size Telescope-South (LST-S) must meet strict dynamic requirements, such as accurate tracking in strong winds and fast repositioning within 20 seconds after a gamma-ray burst alert. A dedicated dynamic model, based on a state-space representation derived from an ANSYS finite element model, was developed to guide critical design decisions and ensure performance compliance. Special attention is given to robust analysis of the main telescope control loops (Bode diagrams as well as H-Infinity approach), considering variations in structural characteristics at different elevation positions and uncertainties in modeling. We address specific challenges such as subsystem time delays, servo-related effects like motor cogging, as well as friction budgeting and modeling with a computationally efficient LuGre model.

Items.Authors: Abhay Kumar, Tanmoy Chattopadhyay
Items.Title: Hard X-Ray Focal-Plane Compton Spectro-Polarimeter: Detector Development and Sensitivity Evaluation
Items.Abstract: The scientific potential of X-ray polarimetry has long been recognized, yet the challenges of measuring polarization have left it largely unexplored, mainly in the hard X-ray regime. With the advent of hard X-ray focusing optics, sensitive focal-plane Compton polarimeters are now feasible. An early example is CXPOL, developed at PRL, which demonstrated 20–80 keV polarimetric capabilities using a plastic scatterer and a CsI(Tl) absorber array.    Performance can be significantly improved by using faster, higher light-yield scintillators such as NaI(Tl) and by employing position-sensitive scatterers and absorbers, enabling simultaneous spectroscopy. We present characterization results from a first position sensitive prototype of NaI(Tl) absorber read out at both ends by SiPMs in coincidence and the sensitivity of the spectro-polarimeter using analytical estimates and Geant4 simulations, demonstrating strong potential for next-generation Compton-based focal-plane spectro-polarimeters.

Items.Authors: D. Christopher Martin, Laura Jones-Wilson, Drew Miles
Items.Title: The Stratospheric Cosmic Web Imager mission overview
Items.Abstract: The Stratospheric Cosmic Web Imager (SCWI) is designed to map, for the first time, the circumgalactic and intergalactic medium (CGM, IGM) in the nearby, low-redshift universe at Lyman alpha, offering extraordinary science at low mission cost. SCWI combines a Caltech-built ultraviolet (UV) integral field spectrograph (IFS) with heritage from the FIREBALL balloon program and ground-based Palomar (PCWI) and Keck (KCWI) Cosmic Web Imagers with the existing JPL-built STABLE telescope and fine pointing system, and a flight-proven JPL-developed photon-counting FIREBALL UV detector. SCWI will perform its first balloon flight in 2028. In addition to the first CGM mapping at near-UV wavelengths, this flight will also flight-prove key payload systems for use on a long-duration superpressure balloon (SPB) flight the following year. The SPB flight wil map emission from the CGM of ~20 nearby galaxies and quasars, and obtain a deep map of the cosmic web at redshift z = 0.7 for the first time.

Items.Authors: Ángel Mato-Martínez, Juan Cozar-Castellano, Antonio Zamora, Gonzalo Moran
Items.Title: EST Optomechanics Preliminary Design
Items.Abstract: The European Solar Telescope (EST) is a 4-meter-class solar telescope that will be installed at the Observatorio del Roque de los Muchachos on La Palma (Spain). In 2025, EST successfully passed its Preliminary Design Review (PDR), confirming that the complete telescope concept has reached sufficient maturity to proceed into detailed design.   A major outcome of the current phase is the completion of the preliminary design for all opto-mechanical elements within the optical train. These elements span from the primary mirror, which collects the incoming solar radiation and focus it on the prime focus, to the coudé light distribution system, which allocates the beam among the different focal stations.  This paper reports the latest updates to the opto-mechanical design of the EST optical train. It summarizes the current baseline design, key design choices, and supporting analyses.

Items.Authors: Juan Carlos Guzman, Louisa Quartermaine, Drew Devereux
Items.Title: From dirt to first image: the Software and Computing systems in SKA-Low AA0.5, report from the trenches and lessons learned
Items.Abstract: The SKA-Low telescope achieved a major milestone in mid 2025, the completion of the Array Assembly 0.5 (AA0.5). This is a 4-station interferometer with the goal of deployment of basic infrastructure, incl. Computing and software at site and in Perth, demonstrating full end to end functionality, including real-time data acquisition and offline calibration and imaging. This paper describes the software and computing systems deployed, the highs and lows and key lessons learned that will help us make progress towards the next stages of the Construction project. This paper will also share the future major challenges and milestones of the software, computing and networking of SKA-Low telescope.

Items.Authors: Andrés Catalán, Rodrigo A. Carrasco, Gonzalo A. Ruz, Juan P. Gil
Items.Title: From Logs to Maintenance Decisions: Explainable Transformer-Based Anomaly Detection and Subsystem Prioritization at Paranal Observatory
Items.Abstract: We present an explainable, log-driven maintenance pipeline built on ESO Paranal Observatory data that links anomalous log messages to subsystem maintenance priorities. A sentiment-aware BERT model classifies each log as normal or anomalous without templates or parsers. Word-level SHAP attributions reveal key terms and are aggregated into a negativity lexicon per subsystem. From this, we construct a decision matrix and rank subsystem criticality with an extended MULTIMOORA method that uses Euclidean reference points and a multiplicative form. Applied to over 5.7 million Very Large Telescope logs, the approach yields stable rankings across weighting schemes and supports concrete actions such as inspections, recalibration, and spare provisioning, and is now integrated into daily maintenance triage.

Items.Authors: Thomas A. Stuber, Steve Ertel, Jacob W. Isbell, Jordan M. Stone, Joshua A. Eisner
Items.Title: Spectrally dispersed non-redundant aperture masking interferometry in L/M band with LBTI/ALES
Items.Abstract: Non redundant aperture masking (NRM) maximizes the angular resolution of a telescope using interferometry. If the interference pattern on the detector can be spectrally dispersed, deeper contrasts and an improved coverage of the Fourier modes, the so-called u-v-plane, can be achieved.  We combined a non-redundant aperture mask with the AO-fed integral field spectrograph ALES of LMIRCam at the Large Binocular Telescope Interferometer (LBTI). Using this setup, we recorded the very first spectrally dispersed NRM observations in the bands L and M (~3µm-5µm), opening up the thermal infrared for this technique. We present the characterization of this novel observing mode based on commissioning data with which we recovered a known close binary star.  This new capability enables LBTI to efficiently survey stars for faint companions or circumstellar disks, which is of great importance for studies on hot exozodiacal dust and target vetting for future exo-Earth imaging missions such as NASA’s HWO.

Items.Authors: Jiangpei Dou, Xi Zhang, Gang Zhao, Mingming Xu, Zhen Wu, Baoning Yuan, Gang Wang, Lingyi Kong, Bo Chen, Shu Jiang, Yongjun Qi, Wei Guo, Di Wang, Ruokun Li, Yiming Zhu, Zhonghua Lv, Bingli Niu, Huihai Wu, Chenming Chang, Cheng Yan, Cheng Wen, Shuwei Miao, Jing Guo, Yinglu Lin, Liping Zheng, Boyang Lv, Weimiao Li
Items.Title: The progress and core science of the Cool Planet Imaging Coronagraph (CPI-C) on Chinese Space-station Survey Telescope (CSST)
Items.Abstract: With over 6200 exoplanets discovered, none Earth-twin has been confirmed. The high-contrast imaging can directly detect the photons from the planet itself, thus open the window for spectroscopy of the atmosphere of the planet, which is crucial to answer “Are we alone in the universe?”. However, the direct imaging technique remains challenge, due to the larger flux ratio contrast and its location very close to the primary star. In this talk, I will introduce progress & scientific goals of CPI-C on CSST, which is dedicated for the high-contrast imaging and characterization of the “COOL” planet. Meanwhile, I will make a brief introduction of the next generation flagship space program of ELSE (Extraterrestrial Life Signal Explorer), which will focus on the direct imaging & spectroscopy of the Earth-mass exoplanets in the HZ of a solar type star, one of the most significant sciences of human beings in this new era.

Items.Authors: Lian Tao
Items.Title: A new vision for the Chasing All Transients Constellation Hunters (CATCH) space mission
Items.Abstract: The Chasing All Transients Constellation Hunters (CATCH) space mission proposes a constellation of over 100 microsatellites equipped with lightweight X-ray optics to address the critical capability gap in follow-up observations for time-domain astronomy. Through intelligent coordination, the constellation will perform multi-target, multi-mode monitoring of astronomical transients. It can further evolve into a distributed network of "wide-field trigger and multi-wavelength follow-up satellites," overcoming the fragmentation and low duty cycle of traditional approaches. CATCH follows a three-phase plan: first, to validate key technologies with several pathfinder satellites; then, to demonstrate intelligent coordination in a small test constellation; and finally, to achieve full operational capability for uninterrupted, all-sky, multi-parameter, and multi-target observations.

Items.Authors: Alexis Carlotti, Steven Martos, David Mouillet, Stéphane Curaba, Jean-Jacques Correia, Marc Ferlet, Alain Delboulbé, Angelie Alagao, Romain Fétick, Vincent Chambouleyron, Arnaud Striffling, Jean-François Sauvage, Benoit Neichel
Items.Title: Exploring the potential of a VIPA spectrograph on-sky
Items.Abstract: We developed a near-IR, échelle-like, fiber-fed spectrograph demonstrator using a VIPA instead of an échelle grating, achieving a high spectral resolution (R=80,000) over a 220 nm range with 38% efficiency (from fiber exit to H2RG detector). Designed to characterize exoplanets at high spectral resolution with an XAO instrument, it was installed in February 2025 for on-sky demonstration at the 1.52m Haute-Provence Observatory telescope, and coupled via the PAPYRUS AO system.    We observed reference and feature-rich stars to test the instrument's H-band transmission and spectral fidelity/stability. K-band tests are planned for early 2026. This presentation covers the current design, calibrations, and on-sky performance, as well as the data reduction pipeline and ETC we developed. We also detail the attempted observation of HR8799c, including a comprehensive SNR analysis to identify limitations and extrapolate to larger telescopes. Finally, we introduce the design of an HK-band version.

Items.Authors: Chung San Chu, Olivier Leblanc, Yves Wiaux
Items.Title: A new concept for compressive radio-interferometric imaging: the modulated rank-one projection model
Items.Abstract: Modern radio-interferometric arrays are to form images with unprecedented sensitivity and resolution. This implies a significant increase in visibility data volumes, which scale as O(Q^2B) for Q antennas and B short-time integration intervals (batches), calling for efficient data dimensionality reduction. We discuss a new approach to data compression during acquisition, coined modulated rank-one projection (MROP). MROP compresses the batchwise covariance matrix into a smaller number of P random ROPs and compresses across time by trading B for a smaller number M of random modulations of the ROP measurement vectors. MROP is validated for monochromatic intensity imaging in simulation and from real data, with comparison to the classical and BDA models, and using the uSARA optimisation algorithm for image formation. Our results suggest that the MROP data size necessary to preserve imaging quality is of the order of image size, well below the original and BDA data sizes.

Items.Authors: Mauro Manetti, Matteo Tintori
Items.Title: The importance of dynamic analysis in mitigating the control-structure-interaction (CSI) in large adaptive deformable mirrors
Items.Abstract: As the size of modern telescopes increases, evaluating Control-Structure Interaction (CSI) becomes critical in the design of large deformable mirrors for Adaptive Optics (AO). Structural resonances can interact with the control system, compromising stability, performance, and the overall robustness of the AO loop.    This work analyzes the coupling between the mirror control system and its supporting structure, extending to the telescope itself. This interaction can trigger vibrations leading to uncontrolled motions—such as tip-tilt, piston, focus, or coma—or inject disturbances back into the telescope. We present numerical tools for analysis across the time, frequency, and Laplace domains to optimize design and characterize system performance. Finally, we demonstrate how incorporating active dampers can significantly enhance the system’s dynamic behavior.

Items.Authors: Giorgio Dho, Davide Fiorina, Paolo Soffitta, Elisabetta Baracchini, Enrico Costa, Fabio Muleri, Stefano Piacentini
Items.Title: Wide-Field Hard X-ray Polarimetry with a Large-Volume TPC
Items.Abstract: We present a wide–field-of-view Time Projection Chamber for hard X-ray polarimetry, derived from technology for directional dark-matter searches. The detector uses a triple-GEM stack and optical readout: secondary scintillation is imaged by a sCMOS camera, enabling 3D reconstruction of photoelectron tracks. The prototype (3.7 cm radius, 6 cm drift) provides track imaging in the 5–50 keV band, with ~15° angular and 10–15% energy resolution between 5 and 45 keV. Calibration with a polarized X-ray beams yields modulation factors at 8.7, 13.0, and 17.4 keV, exceeding 0.4 at 17 keV. We outline a next-generation chamber to explore gas mixtures and pressures, a machine-learning–based pipeline for onboard data reduction, and first estimates of background and signal-to-noise for Crab-like sources in low Earth orbit. This flexible platform targets high-energy transients such as GRBs and magnetar flares and, with a narrow-field collimator, can monitor Galactic sources down to flux ≳100 mCrab.

Items.Authors: Stephanie A. Rossini-Bryson, Barnaby Norris, Elizabeth Arcadi, Julien Lozi, Sébastien Vievard, Vincent Déo, David Sweeney, Glen Douglass, Mona Elmorsy, Eckhart Spalding, Michael Withford, Simon Gross, Peter Tuthill, Olivier Guyon
Items.Title: The GLINT instrument: demonstrating on-sky photonic nulling and fringe tracking for next-generation interferometry
Items.Abstract: The Guided Light Interferometric Nulling Technology (GLINT) instrument on the SCExAO system at the Subaru Telescope performs photonic nulling interferometry using an integrated chip to achieve compact and stable high-contrast performance. Recent upgrades to its optical train, control architecture, and photonic tricoupler design now enable simultaneous nulling and phase retrieval for fringe tracking. We present the first on-sky demonstration of closed-loop fringe tracking using tricoupler outputs, implemented within the MILK/CACAO real-time control framework, driving a deformable mirror at kHz speeds to stabilise the interferometric null. We also show spectrally dispersed null-depth measurements from GLINT’s science channels, for a range of astronomical targets. These results demonstrate improved nulling stability and confirm integrated-photonics-based nullers as promising technology for future ELT and space interferometry missions.

Items.Authors: Nicholas E. Thomas
Items.Title: The HEROIX broadband X-ray space telescope mission concept
Items.Abstract: The High EneRgy Observatory for Imaging X-rays (HEROIX) Medium-Class Mission concept envisions a next-generation broadband X-ray observatory designed to meet the astrophysics community’s need for high-angular-resolution studies of the Cosmic X-ray Background. Building on the science legacy of NASA’s NuSTAR mission and more than 30 years of advances in replicated NiCo shell technology at NASA Marshall, HEROIX proposes a space observatory comprising four co-aligned telescopes achieving 5 arcsecond half-power diameter (HPD) angular resolution. This capability, approached by the resolution demonstrated in the FOXSI-4 sounding rocket mission and under development through the SuperHERO balloon mission, will be extended to energies up to 80 keV through multilayer coatings. Marshall’s inhouse precision optics manufacturing enables an integrated effective area of 380 cm² at 30 keV, which, combined with high-resolution optics, opens new windows into extreme astrophysical non-thermal processes.
